452.t: Told in New York he needs a second spinal operation
452.s: In 1947, with three months of bookings and cars bought, a doctor tells Cobb the operation must be repeated; he drives bitterly to dinner at Joe Thomas's home.
452.q: I'll tell you how it happened. I'm at 124th and Madison Avenue in a hospital for [joint]disease, for my second spinal operation, which made me bitter. I had 3 months of bookings, but let me back up a minute.

452.t: Fifteen and a half months flat on his back
452.s: Complications, a hip problem and repeated casts and ambulance trips stretch the recovery to fifteen and a half months, two and a half years out of work.
452.q: No, it was longer than that. That's what the doctor said, 9 months. And complications did set in. He told me to lay in bed like, when I rolled over, roll like a log, on account of the spine. And he didn't put me in no

452.t: Hartford doctors send him home and Dr. Mayer takes over again
452.s: Refusing amputation, Cobb is sent home by ambulance, stays in bed through the summer, then enters Hospital for Joint Disease under Dr. Mayer from October 1956 to January 1957.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: No, they did not. They told me that they may have to take this leg because it wasn't forming calcium as fast as this one. So I told them that let me live with it a little longer and let me give it a chance because I wasn't going to let them take nothing. So they got a little indignant, I guess,…

452.t: Going back to work despite doctors' warnings
452.s: Cobb says the doctors once said he'd die, but trusting God he returned to work with Dr. Mayer's permission; his first job was Philadelphia's 21 Club in a walking cast, earning the nickname Speedy.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: So the doctor said that. The doctor said I was going to die too, didn't he? But I'm just a firm believer that there's a God above, and whatever he wants me to do and give me that strength, I'm going to do it.

452.t: Nine months bedridden: breaking the news to the band and losing money on the cars
452.s: Back in the doctor's office he is told to lie flat for nine months, then tells his band in August 1947 and takes a loss on the cars.
452.q: Yeah, all right. We're back in the doctor's office now, and he told me, he said "You're not in your teens anymore and we're dealing with a bone situation, and nature takes a little longer to heal them." And so he said, and this is what hurt me -- "My advice to you is that you're gonna have to lay.…

452.t: Back and hip unharmed; Lisette's first birthday
452.s: Cobb says the fused areas held and only the leg was damaged; he left the hospital the day after his daughter's first birthday and did not work until June 1957.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: I don't have any problem with my back. I don't have any problem today with my hip. Wherever they fused it, that's the strongest part of your body. Won't give an inch. I never had any more problems with my hip, never had any more problems, through that accident and the impact, nothing changed with…

452.t: Pott's disease and the March 1948 operation
452.s: Cobb explains the bone fusion operation he entered on March 1, 1948, how a fall and a car injury together caused the disease, and that he stayed out two and a half years.
452.ch: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
452.q: Pott's disease came from a lick. Well, I already suffered with my back, I told you, from when I got hit by the car coming out of the theater and running back, and couldn't see (inaudible) and run into the traffic, and the man hit me. All right, I suffered through the years on that. And he come and…

452.t: A new seven-piece band and learning to play on crutches
452.s: Cobb forms a seven-piece band with Dickie Harris, Harold Cumberbatch and Eddie Lewis (nicknamed Tiger), and explains how he still needs crutches on steps.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: Baritone, trombone -- Dickie Harris was on the band, and I had Harold Cumberbatch back out of Brooklyn. Eddy Lewis was still with me on trumpet.

452.t: Therapy in the pool, a shorter leg and a built-up shoe
452.s: After the cast, Cobb relearns movement, discovers the Hartford surgeons left his leg short, and gets a lift in his shoe made first in leather and then cork.
452.ch: On the road, James Brown and the 1956 crash
452.q: Yeah, well, I mean I had to go and -- and, you know, when they cut -- when Dr. Mayer cut that cast off me in the Hospital for Joint Disease, everything I had for muscle, all my skin just fell on the bed. I didn't have no muscle. And he sent a therapist up to me to take exercises. I had rotating…

452.t: Convalescing at home with Dr. Mayer's exercises
452.s: Dr. Mayer visited Cobb's Long Island house and gave him seven weeks of exercises so he could walk on a walker and crutches.
452.ch: Leaving Hampton and starting his own band
452.q: -- I come out for convalescing. My doctor came to my house -- something unusual -- I'm living in Long Island, Jamaica, that is, Brick Town, and Dr. Mayer came out to my house and gave me exercises for seven weeks to get me prepared to get up out of bed. He tested my spine with his thumb going down…

452.t: Consulting doctors and Dr. Mayer's diagnosis of Pott's disease
452.s: Cobb gets a second opinion; Dr. Mayer, with agent Ben Barth present, diagnoses Pott's disease and warns of nine months in bed.
452.q: So I knew I had to tell my agent; I had to call him from somewhere, so I opened up and told them. Then I called my agent, and he was the man who suggested (unintelligible) and he said, "Are you sure?" And I said, "I'll tell you what the man said." So we had a consultation -- I spent $85 and went to…

452.t: Falling ill in Dallas with pleurisy and nearly dying
452.s: Cobb takes sick on a trip to Dallas, is brought home at 119 pounds, and is found to have pleurisy; a doctor treats him at home and in Jefferson Davis Hospital.
452.ch: First bands, illness and Houston life
452.q: ... pieces. And we went up to Dallas, and I took sick up there. And I was a guy that believed in taking my money and putting it in a sock, and putting a safety pin in it, and when I put the safety pin in it, that means one thing. Don't spend it. But I neglected myself, and took sick. I didn't eat…

76.s: They hadn't seen a doctor in years; the last, Dr. MacDonald, who also treated Pee Wee Russell, told Zutty to put on his clothes and get out, and Dance is offered cakes.
76.q: Put on your clothes and get the hell out of here! That's what he told me.

76.t: Marge's closed esophagus and the operation
76.s: Through Dick Kennedy they got Dr. MacDonald for Marge, whose esophagus had completely closed from nervous tension that began in Europe; an operation at St. Clare's saved her.
76.q: And this doctor that we were going to had taken exrays. I had had the GI series and all of that. And so after Dick Kennedy told Zutty to take me over to Doctor MacDonald. Doctor MacDonald told Zutty he would have to call this doctor and tell him he was letting him go you know for the ethics of…

76.t: Marshall Brown's loudspeakers blamed for the hypertension
76.s: Marge believes the loud electronic equipment Marshall Brown placed next to Zutty's drums at his job, leaving him unable to hear, raised his blood pressure.
76.q: And he was on the other end and all the noise was going into Zutty's ears, you know. With this electronic equipment, where he was blowing his trombone and all. And Zutty would come home every night

76.t: A dizzy spell in the five-and-ten a week earlier
76.s: Marge recalls Zutty nearly fainted buying wrapping paper at the five-and-ten a week before, which they put down to heat; the cause was hypertension they didn't know he had.
76.q: But the week before Zutty went over to the 5 and 10 to get some wrapping paper and cards. We had had a big slab of bacon sent to us Smithfield bacon from Virginia. And we couldn't eat it all so we sent half of it to my sister's. And Zutty said, well send it to Sis, half of it. He went to get the…

76.t: Refusing the spinal tap and nursing him at home
76.s: Marge refused the spinal tap and took Zutty home despite the hospital's anger, kept him on a salt-free diet with Dr. Newman, though they first ate Chinese food, and Zutty was told not to drink.
76.q: And he said, so I said to him, well what are you going to do to him? He said, we have a bed for you upstairs. And I said, well what are you going to do to him. He said, well we'll give him the spinal tap. Well I knew I wasn't going to let them give him no spinal tap. And Zutty said he didn't want…

76.t: Waiting hours at the Veterans' Hospital
76.s: After Dr. Murphy suggested the Veterans' Hospital, Marge got Zutty there by cab in snow and ice and they waited from 2:30 to 8 pm; the neurologist found a clot on the left side, a slight stroke.
76.q: And Doctor Murphy said it sounds like a stroke. And so he said, I'm going to call the Veteran's Hospital and you take him down. And he called me back, said I'll call you back. Said you have Zutty down there around one o'clock, don't rush.

84.t: St. Louis, Springfield and illness back home
84.s: After the Louisiana Shakers, Handy went to St. Louis and Springfield, fell sick with stomach trouble, and ran a business at home.
84.q: No, I left St. Louis and I went to Springfield. I played out in Springfield for six, seven months out there. And I got sick. Matter of fact, I was sick when I went there. And I had to leave Springfield to come back in because I was about dying on my feet up there with my stomach. And I left and…

84.t: Returning from illness, restaurant, and resuming playing
84.s: After Springfield he ran a restaurant and bar for two and a half years before playing again.
84.q: Well, I come in, I opened up a restaurant and a ball. Uh-oh. Right across the track there. And I stayed around here about two and a half years. You play anything? No, I couldn't play nothing. I had a bad stomach, I couldn't do nothing. I left and went back to New Orleans. And that's where I started…

84.s: Handy describes how stomach pain interrupted playing, drinking soda water on the bandstand, and its origin in childhood illness.
84.q: No, it stops you from playing and pains yourself. Yeah, it's a pain. I remember when I was playing to LeVito at Lee Collins and then, I had a quarter of whiskey on this side and a quarter of cooking soda water on this side. I'd be standing up taking the soda on my horn and boom. When the pains hit…

84.t: St. Louis sidemen, Sleepy's trumpet surprise, illness and Springfield
84.s: Handy recalls New Orleans men in St. Louis, the second trumpeter who outplayed Guy Kelly, his illness in hospital around 1938-39, and a small band in Springfield.
84.q: No. Uh, Gishard, he's from here, but he was playing with another band on the name of Eddie. Eddie something they was playing. He's a saxophone player too, a how-to player. And he had a brother, a dead shawty, played bass, but I think the young ones did the bass play. I think he died. I had a fellow…

470.t: The 1953 car accident and the dislocated jaw that ended his trombone playing
470.s: Thrown through a windshield returning from Lake Hamilton, Baker spent a week in a coma, then years later discovered he had played on a dislocated jaw and had to quit trombone around 1960-61.
470.ch: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
470.q: I mean April – is an infant. But let me back up – yeah, because it’s coming later. Basically, that takes us up through 1959, ’60. But let me back up to something that really turns out to have a major impact on my life. In 1953, coming back from Lake Hamilton when we played up there, I’m coming back

470.t: Two years without an instrument and the wired jaw
470.s: Without a playable instrument he played gigs on piano under heavy medication, had his jaw wired for six weeks, and began cello with Mr. Brown's encouragement.
470.ch: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
470.q: So the playing thing – then, once I was in the hospital, I was without an instrument for at least two years, without an instrument that I could play, because my face was gone. I couldn’t play that [trombone]. Piano was resisting me, even though I did play gigs on piano. I played some gigs on bass…

470.t: Giving up the trombone for good
470.s: Baker returned to cello, and the doctors' warning about losing his facial muscles and barbecue persuaded him to stop playing trombone.
470.ch: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
470.q: Oh, I was so happy not to be able to play trombone. I just thought, wow, this is really great, not being able to play trombone. Maybe I’ll . . . [laughter]

470.t: Hospital stays, the psychiatric ward anecdote, then piano, bass and cello
470.s: He tried to play long tones in a hospital ward, then practiced piano and bass and was given a pawn-shop cello by Mr. Brown.
470.ch: A broken jaw and the switch to cello
470.q: severing the buxtinator [buccinator] muscles, which are the muscles which open and close your mouth, and then see if they could retrain other muscles to do the job. Fortunately, the doctor that I was with said, “No. We’re not going to do anything that is irreversible.” So I spent time in and out…

170.s: A friend takes him to Bellevue where TB is found, and he is sent to the Veterans Hospital at Castle Point.
170.ch: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
170.q: this was about in '62; I was gigging, around, you know, just little gigs here and there. In 1963 I got so I couldn't go up stairs; I'd get out of breath, you know, I was coming down with TB. You know, I always believed that you had TB, you'd be spitting up blood, but it hadn't reached that stage,…

170.t: Chicago with Clifford Jordan and Klook, September 1976
170.s: Ill and gasping for breath, Ware plays the Jazz Showcase with Jordan.
170.q: But anyway, after that record date and Detroit gig, Cliff called me one day and said, 'Well, man, we got five days in Chicago.' Now, that was last --

170.t: The Foxhole gig and collapsed lungs
170.s: Ware plays the Foxhole with Wilbur Campbell and Sam Dockery; his lung collapses several times; he records with Walt Dickerson.
170.q: Sam Dockery on piano and we had a surprise guest, Babs Gonzales come up, just to sing with us. But before this could come about, my lung collapsed on me. It frightened me, but stayed in the hospital for about seven or eight days and they inflated it again and I felt good, better than I did in…

170.t: Released in 1961, recording for Blue Note and failing health
170.s: After jail, Ware cleans up during the drug panic, records for Blue Note with Grant Green and Hank Mobley, and his health fails.
170.ch: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
170.q: When I come out, just before that, a great big snowstorm hit New York, and I'm out there in a summer suit; this was about in '61, and anyway, A Jones A was working over there at a hotel with somebody, and anyway, I come out and a friend of mine, Billy Howell, a trombone player, living on the upper…

127.t: Recovery, diet and blowing trumpet again
127.s: Punch describes the surgery, his health, daily practice, sitting in on trumpet recently and his diet.
127.q: Well, I wouldn't say they're trying to give me medicine to pass it out, because the doctors were taking extra of me every day and they couldn't find out what we were on. Took me all kind of ways, couldn't find me. They did find out they laid about six or four little pillars, you know? And told me…

127.t: Gallstone illness that began on tour in Pensacola
127.s: Punch tells of rice pudding in Pensacola, a doctor's warning about gallstones, his fear of surgery, and the hospital stay.
127.q: Well, I'll tell you about that. The same little show I was been to called the Browns Mannequins. That had been a few years back. Now more than, I'd been more than 12 years. I had ate a piece of some rice pudding in Pensacola, Florida. I was going from Pensacola to Nashville. It was a good gym, see?…

127.t: Recent contact with Louis and talk about his illness
127.s: Punch says he saw Louis at last year's festival and gets mail from him; the interviewers will contact Lucille and mention both men are sick.
127.ch: Brass bands and Louis in New Orleans
127.q: Louis? Uh, I'll be there last viester.

555.t: Going back East and her fear after the stroke
555.s: She plans to return to New York, and admits being afraid to see people for years after the stroke for fear of pity.
555.q: I was afraid to go out and see everybody – anybody, until six months ago or something like that, because . . .

555.t: Recovering from the stroke, helped by Randy
555.s: After the stroke one must relearn everything; Randy and her mother pushed her and Randy got her writing again.
555.q: Oh yeah, but Randy helped me to get started writing, and so I’m doing it. I’m not writing as fast and all of that as I . . .

555.t: Missing her horn after the stroke
555.s: Liston promises to blow again but gets only a few notes with her damaged slide arm and exercises it daily.
555.q: Yeah, but I got to – I have this arm. I don’t know what to do with this. I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t . . .

80.t: Playing trumpet in the hospital for ice cream; leaving Phillipsburg
80.s: In hospital he played 'Mockingbird' to get ice cream from the dietician, kept his embouchure in shape, and eventually left Phillipsburg to come home.
80.ch: Postwar years, accident and lean times
80.q: I used to play so she -- yeah. She liked 'Mockingbird', so I used to rah dah doo dee dah, and she send me some icecream.

80.t: Glaucoma, cataracts and the possibility of a cornea transplant
80.s: Poor health, hospital stays and glaucoma and cataracts made him leave the band, and doctors have discussed a cornea transplant.
80.q: Well, I have glaucoma, and cataracts, and all that junk. And the left eye, the -- they're talking -- they're still talking about doing a -- a cornea transplant.

80.t: Discovering the 25-year-old hip pin had broken
80.s: Doctors found by accident that the pin put in his hip in 1950 had broken, though he felt no difference until recently.
80.q: Well, when they put it in there 25 years ago, 1950, they told me, some day it would go, you know. And so aw, what the hell. Wherever I'd be, by then I figured 25 years is -- you know.

231.t: The 1967 stroke at the Americana Hotel
231.s: After a Sunday night show with Judy Garland he woke Tuesday unable to lift his left hand, walked into the hospital and left in a wheelchair.
231.ch: Television, the stroke and later reflections
231.q: No career. That's the end of that. Stop right there. Stop right there. What am I going to do? Go ahead, help me out. You help me. If you could help me, very good.

231.t: Pneumonia, Buck and Willie Bryant, and working alone
231.s: When Bubbles had pneumonia, Buck worked briefly with Willie Bryant and they staged a holdup story to keep Nazarro from taking the money.
231.q: Yeah, because they came -- I wasn't in the hospital, I was at home. After they did the show they come by my house to see me and they told me the story about them staging the holdup and said they were robbed. They told me about that.

231.t: The spastic leg and twelve years of nothing
231.s: He says it was the spastic leg that ended his dancing, and inadequate therapy and 12 idle years followed.
231.ch: Television, the stroke and later reflections
231.q: No, I don't know that. I don't know that. I don't know that at all. How did I know it? I don't either. My arm didn't stop my profession. I didn't care

418.t: The Lester Young record date and illness with pneumonia and ulcer
418.s: He made records with Lester in California and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.
418.ch: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
418.q: Yeah. Yeah. Right after that I got sick so I didn't know whether Norman wanted me to stay with the group or not. I wasn't able to anyway. So that was that.

418.t: The Lester Young record date and illness with pneumonia and ulcer
418.s: He made records with Lester in California for Norman Granz and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.
418.q: Yes. Yeah, right after that I got sick. So I didn't know whether Norman wanted me to stay with the group or not. But I wasn't able to anyway, so that was that.

418.t: The Lester Young record date and illness with pneumonia and ulcer
418.s: He made records with Lester in California and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.
418.q: Yeah. Yeah. Right after that I got sick so I didn't know whether Norman wanted me to stay with the group or not. I wasn't able to anyway. So that was that.

387.t: Waiting for the phone and the 1966 heart attack
387.s: After three idle years he had a heart attack.
387.q: I don't even think they think, but I have also learned that when I go around looking for things, nothing happens. You like to do that? That's nice, but they never call.

387.s: Illness ended his ambition; he recovered intermittently until 1951.
387.q: If I had had any ambition before that, if I had any proclivity to be ambitious, that just knocked it out of me. It caused me to read a lot and I don't regret it, but it was a lot of years sitting around.

387.s: Powell also got TB; Sauter says they were never friends.
387.q: He was on a plane and he had a hemorrhage on a plane. Mel Powell was in that too; who knows if that didn't kick off Mel Powell.

288.t: How he fell ill and gave up the horn; insurance work
288.s: He describes doctors, the nerve trouble in his lip, and a sick policyholder's symptoms that frightened him.
288.ch: Society work, Camilla Todd and Storyville
288.q: you know, it's like if you was in the woods, you know. You know, that man still could play that funk before he's singing that. When we got through, I'm telling you, those people, bah bah bah bah bah bah bah bah bah. I told Chick, I said Chick, I got him. Will your doctor let you play anymore? Well…

288.t: Illness in 1924-25 at the New Orleans Country Club; giving up the horn
288.s: Charles describes the spell that struck him leading his orchestra at afternoon tea, and the Maple Leaf band's violin and clarinet players.
288.q: I don't have it no more. I gave it up the very time that I gave up music, I gave it up. You see I got sick in 1924. Well I'll declare. And in 25 the doctor claimed that I would never be able to handle that instrument anymore. Is that right? And I went through it anyhow. I played it up until 25. You…

571.t: George Lewis's health on the stand
571.s: Rockwell recalls Lewis being ill and having a slight heart attack on the stand but finishing the night.
571.q: um george george was sick off and on during this time and he would have i remember this one time he had a heart attack right on the stand a slight heart attack you know and they would tell say well get off you know but he would just stay right there and finish the finish the night and then…

571.s: Lewis gives his weight around 121 pounds, and how it fell after an operation and low blood counts. They compare it with the weight of a coffee sack.
571.ch: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
571.q: I weighed around about 121. And how much did you weigh? Then I started losing weight. After I got operated on the, I was already in the stomach, I started losing, and I got onto 114 and I stayed there, I continued working, and then all the days I started, blood counts got bad, and I don't know, I…

783.t: Two lost years and joining Al Wynn's band
783.s: He sums up losing his horn for two years after the lip operation, and says Al Wynn and Frankie coaxed him back into a small group about three years ago.
783.ch: Closing and the Al Wynn band
783.q: you see that's about all you see the only thing I lost track was those two years I lost my horn when I had the operation on my lip well you're lucky to come through that right and get your lip back that's right you see and then you see usually when I feel like people lost track of me as playing as…

783.t: Cancer on his lip, 1926, and joining Charlie Elgar at the Savoy
783.s: He leaves Oliver in February 1926 for treatment of lip cancer, is off the horn two years, then plays with Charlie Elgar at the Savoy Ballroom with Manuel Perez.
783.q: Egypt, everything. Yeah, that's it. So that's where he comes up. What it was, something happened between him and Bonnie and you don't know what happened. So that was causing that. Then that's all that's going on now and the band is still together up until 1926. In 1926 in February, I had to leave…

576.t: The Blue Note album Portrait and a planned Fred Astaire project
576.s: She says she was sick during the 1962 Blue Note album, and describes an unrecorded bass-and-voice Fred Astaire tribute with Cameron Brown.
576.q: This one? I have a whole new thing on this, with the bass. I do a whole thing on this with all dance tunes, dedicated to Fred Astaire. Bass and voice. Yeah. It’s never been recorded yet. But I will record it one day.

576.t: Singing the record during an ectopic pregnancy
576.s: She was seriously ill with an undiagnosed ectopic pregnancy during the session, with Steve Swallow and Barry Galbraith supportive.
576.ch: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
576.q: I have no clue what it was. But, but I know that, uh, I know that, um, I was very sick when I did that, uh, that recording, because I had an ectopic pregnancy. I was with this… one of the creeps I was involved with in my life, who will remain unmentionable. Uh, but I didn‟t know I was pregnant, you…

409.s: Taken ill after playing A Train, Cootie was sent home by Dr. Arthur Logan, hospitalised, and told to rest a year.
409.q: Yeah. We was playing up at the race track. We played the matinee. I went out to play the "A Train". I come back to my seat, and they wanted me to take a bow, and I couldn't hardly get up to take a bow.

409.t: Dr. Logan's death and Duke's last illness
409.s: Dr. Arthur Logan's death was a blow; Duke was sick on his last trip and Cootie sent prayers via Mercer.
409.q: Yeah. That last trip we was on. See, he was working night by night. And I know he was sick. He was just barely making it. He told Mercer don't take the bus too far away from him, because he may have to leave any minute, to come home. That's when he left to come home.

378.t: Hearing loss and the ear operation
378.s: In Palm Springs he realized his hearing was failing, had an operation, and thought he'd never play again.
378.ch: Las Vegas, Sinatra and later years
378.q: -- and I had the operation and I thought 'Well, I'll never play again, and I guess I can tell you about how I got back in playing. I had really give up the idea that I'd ever play again.

378.s: He fell ill with typhoid in Los Angeles at nineteen; Orpheum booking agents cared for him in a hotel across from the Biltmore, and he lost his hair.
378.ch: West Coast trip and Mildred's circle
378.q: Went out to the West Coast, we played Seattle, and we played down the Coast, down to Los Angeles. And then I got sick in Los Angeles, I got typhoid fever.

89.t: Cataracts, a walk-out from surgery and the decision to leave Puerto Rico
89.s: Nearly blind from cataracts, he fled the operating table after being strapped down, and chose Las Vegas for the surgery.
89.q: : After ten years I wanted to come home, you know, you come home to your roots and it's -- I don't care how good things are. I left a good salary there -- a tremendous salary that I was getting, and I left it -- band, salary and just moved everything, all my furniture and brought it here. Just…

89.t: Driving across the country nearly blind and the operation in Las Vegas
89.s: His family read road signs as he drove from Jacksonville to Las Vegas, and the cataract operation on September 28 succeeded.
89.q: Oh, I did. Now, here's what happened. I was tricked. At the hospital, they had given me -- put drops in some sort of solution in my eyes that temporarily cleared them up and they stayed clear for about a week. And I said, "Well, I've got it made, my eyes are going to clear up." And it lasted until…

70.t: The 1966 neck operation and Bell's palsy
70.s: After a lot of New York work, an operation on a neck growth left Jackson with Bell's palsy, and he could not play until 1969.
70.q: I had been playing the Americana all the time, the Copa. I had done two Broadway shows. By then I had done Fade Out, Fade In. I had done Gigi Jeanmaire when she was over here from Europe. It was a fantastic show. And I was playing bass at [ ]. I was playing behind different vocalists. And I was…

70.t: Not blaming the surgeon, determined to play again
70.s: Doctors said the nerve surgery was tedious and not the surgeon's fault; Jackson vowed no one could stop his music and Hinton praises his comeback.
70.q: I think it was an unfortunate thing. I don't think it was an accident of the surgeon because I've talked to different doctors since then and they said not to blame him.

120.t: Offered Milwaukee's Wisconsin Ballroom and falling gravely ill
120.s: Carl Dunbar brings him to Milwaukee, but on opening night he collapses with intestinal flu and a near breakdown and stays with Dunbar a month.
120.q: Yeah - the Wisconsin River, and it seems like bad luck was following me around a little bit about that time; I went--- we organized this very good band rehearsed it and I had never been sick a day in my life at this point and the first night of the opening, I got something terribly wrong with my…

120.t: Forming a band for the Chateau Country Club
120.s: From a sickbed he phones Milwaukee musicians, rehearses in the ballroom and plays three weeks that stretch to eight months.
120.q: Oh, yeah, but can you imagine that - I couldn't get out of bed; I was really sicker than hell-- and I had never been sick before that. So, in the meantime, there was a guy that had a place called "The Chateau Country Club" in Milwaukee and he called me and said --- listen, how would you like to put…
